subject: Everyday Science
q: Fraudulent emails or websites that imitate trusted organisations to steal passwords or bank details are known as:
explanation: Phishing tricks people into giving away sensitive information by pretending to be a bank, company or other trusted source.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A firewall protects a computer network by:
o: Monitoring and blocking unauthorised network traffic
explanation: A firewall checks incoming and outgoing traffic against security rules and blocks connections that are not allowed.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Malware that locks or encrypts a victim’s files and demands payment to restore them is called:
explanation: Ransomware holds data hostage, which is why regular offline backups are an important defence.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Converting data into a coded form so that only authorised people can read it is called:
explanation: Encryption scrambles data using a key; only someone with the correct key can decrypt and read it.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Two-factor authentication improves account security by:
o: Using two different passwords of the same kind
Requiring a second proof of identity in addition to the password
Allowing two users to share one account
explanation: Combining something you know (a password) with something you have, such as a code sent to your phone, stops attackers who have only stolen the password.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A Denial-of-Service (DoS) attack aims to:
o: Steal a user’s password by guessing
Make a website or server unavailable by flooding it with traffic
Encrypt a user’s files for ransom
explanation: By overwhelming a server with requests, a DoS attack prevents genuine users from reaching the service.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The purpose of a CAPTCHA test on websites is to:
o: Speed up the loading of pages
Tell human users apart from automated programs
explanation: CAPTCHAs set small tasks that are easy for humans but hard for bots, preventing automated sign-ups and spam.

subject: Everyday Science
q: On the web, “cookies” are:
o: Viruses that damage the hard disk
Small data files that websites store in a user’s browser
explanation: Cookies remember information such as login status and preferences between visits to a website.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Who is the founder of Wikipedia?
explanation: Jimmy Wales launched Wikipedia, the free online encyclopedia, in 2001 (with Larry Sanger); Julian Assange founded WikiLeaks.

subject: Everyday Science
q: In a relational database, data is organised into:
explanation: Each table stores records as rows and fields as columns, and tables are linked by common fields.

subject: Everyday Science
q: DBMS stands for:
explanation: A DBMS is software for creating, storing, retrieving and managing data in databases.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Buying and selling goods and services over the internet is called:
explanation: Electronic commerce covers online shopping, payments and business transactions carried out over the internet.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A website that finds information on the web when you type in keywords is called a:
explanation: Search engines index billions of web pages and return the ones most relevant to the keywords entered.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Mobile phones communicate with cell towers using:
explanation: Mobile phones send and receive signals as radio (microwave-frequency) electromagnetic waves to and from nearby base stations.

subject: Everyday Science
q: GSM, a widely used mobile phone standard, stands for:
explanation: GSM is the second-generation digital mobile standard that introduced SIM cards and SMS text messaging worldwide.

subject: Everyday Science
q: SIM, as in a mobile phone’s SIM card, stands for:
explanation: The SIM card stores the subscriber’s identity and security keys that let the network recognise the user.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Optical fibre cables carry data in the form of:
explanation: Data is coded as flashes of light that travel along thin glass fibres, giving very high speeds with little interference.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The telephone was invented by:
explanation: Bell was granted the first US patent for the telephone in 1876.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Long-distance wireless (radio) telegraphy was pioneered by:
explanation: Marconi developed practical radio communication and sent signals across the Atlantic in 1901.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Making voice calls over the internet instead of ordinary telephone lines is known as:
explanation: Voice over Internet Protocol converts speech into data packets sent across the internet, as used by many calling apps.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The “G” in 4G and 5G mobile networks stands for:
explanation: Each “generation” marks a major step in mobile technology, from analogue 1G to today’s high-speed 5G.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Second-generation computers replaced vacuum tubes with:
explanation: Transistors were smaller, faster, cooler and more reliable than vacuum tubes, which had been used in the first generation.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The microprocessor, a complete CPU on a single chip, is the feature of which generation of computers?
explanation: First-generation computers used vacuum tubes, the second transistors, the third integrated circuits and the fourth microprocessors.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Who is known as the “father of the computer”?
explanation: In the 19th century Babbage designed the Analytical Engine, a mechanical general-purpose computer, earning him this title.

subject: Everyday Science
q: One of the earliest general-purpose electronic digital computers, completed in 1945, was:
explanation: ENIAC, built at the University of Pennsylvania, used about 18,000 vacuum tubes and filled a large room.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Machine learning is sub area of:
explanation: Machine learning is the branch of AI in which systems improve at a task by learning patterns from data rather than following fixed rules.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which of the following is a branch of AI focused on enabling machines to understand and process human language?
explanation: NLP deals with understanding and generating human language, as in translation tools, voice assistants and chatbots.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The term “artificial intelligence” was coined in 1956 by:
explanation: McCarthy used the term in the proposal for the 1956 Dartmouth conference, regarded as the founding event of AI as a field.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The Turing test is used to judge whether a machine can:
o: Store more data than a human brain
Show behaviour indistinguishable from that of a human
explanation: Proposed by Alan Turing in 1950, the test asks whether a human judge in conversation can tell the machine from a person.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The field of AI that enables computers to interpret and understand images and videos is called:
explanation: Computer vision powers face recognition, medical image analysis and self-driving cars by extracting meaning from visual data.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A software program that simulates conversation with users through text or voice is called a:
explanation: Chatbots use language processing to understand user messages and respond automatically, for example in customer service.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Deep learning is a type of machine learning based on:
o: Artificial neural networks with many layers
explanation: Deep networks stack many layers of artificial neurons, each learning more abstract features from the data.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Artificial neural networks are loosely inspired by the structure of the:
explanation: They consist of interconnected “neurons” that pass signals and adjust connection strengths as they learn, much as brain cells do.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Training an AI model on examples that are already labelled with the correct answers is called:
explanation: In supervised learning the model learns the relationship between inputs and known outputs, such as emails labelled “spam” or “not spam”.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A computer program that imitates the decision-making of a human specialist using a knowledge base of rules is called an:
explanation: Expert systems apply stored rules and facts from experts to give advice, for example in medical diagnosis.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Technology that converts spoken words into written text is called:
explanation: Speech recognition analyses sound patterns to identify words; speech synthesis is the reverse, turning text into speech.

subject: Everyday Science
q: AI systems that create new content such as text, images or music are known as:
explanation: Generative AI models learn patterns from large amounts of data and use them to produce original output in response to prompts.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The term “big data” refers to:
o: Data stored on large hard disks only
Extremely large and complex data sets that need special tools to analyse
explanation: Big data is characterised by huge volume, speed and variety, beyond the capacity of ordinary software to process.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Discovering useful patterns and relationships in large collections of data is called:
explanation: Data mining uses statistics and machine learning to find trends, for example in customer purchases or disease spread.

subject: Everyday Science
q: GIS stands for:
explanation: A Geographic Information System links data to locations on the Earth so that it can be mapped and analysed.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A Geographic Information System (GIS) is mainly used to:
o: Capture, store, analyse and display location-based data
explanation: GIS combines maps with data layers, such as roads, population and land use, to support planning and decision-making.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Obtaining information about the Earth’s surface without physical contact, for example from satellites, is called:
explanation: Remote sensing uses sensors on satellites or aircraft to record reflected or emitted energy from the Earth’s surface.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which of the following is an active remote sensing system, because it sends out its own signal and records the return?
o: A photographic satellite relying on sunlight
explanation: Active sensors like radar emit energy and measure its reflection, so they work day and night and through clouds; passive sensors rely on sunlight.

subject: Everyday Science
q: RADAR stands for:
explanation: Radar sends out radio waves and times their echoes to find the distance, direction and speed of objects.

subject: Everyday Science
q: LiDAR measures distances and creates detailed 3D maps by using:
explanation: LiDAR times how long laser pulses take to bounce back, producing precise elevation and terrain models.

subject: Everyday Science
q: In GIS, roads, rivers and boundaries stored as points, lines and polygons are an example of which data model?
explanation: The vector model uses coordinates to represent discrete features; the raster model stores data as a grid of cells, like satellite images.

subject: Everyday Science
q: GPS stands for:
explanation: GPS is a satellite navigation system that gives location and time information anywhere on Earth.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The GPS satellite navigation system was developed and is operated by:
explanation: GPS was built by the US Department of Defense and is operated by the US Space Force; other countries have their own systems.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A GPS receiver needs signals from at least how many satellites to fix a three-dimensional position (latitude, longitude and altitude)?
explanation: Three satellites give position by trilateration, and a fourth is needed to correct the receiver’s clock error, so at least four are required for a 3D fix.

subject: Everyday Science
q: BeiDou is the satellite navigation system of:
explanation: BeiDou is China’s global navigation satellite system; Russia operates GLONASS and the European Union operates Galileo.

subject: Everyday Science
q: GLONASS is a global satellite navigation system operated by:
explanation: GLONASS is Russia’s counterpart to GPS, and many receivers use both systems together for better accuracy.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Using storage, servers and software over the internet on demand, instead of on one’s own computer, is called:
explanation: Cloud providers run large data centres and let users rent computing resources over the internet as needed.

subject: Everyday Science
q: In cloud computing, SaaS stands for:
explanation: With SaaS, users access complete applications, such as web-based email, through a browser without installing them.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Renting virtual servers, storage and networks from a cloud provider is which cloud service model?
explanation: IaaS provides the basic computing infrastructure, on which customers install and manage their own operating systems and software.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A blockchain is best described as a:
o: Chain of computers connected by cables
Shared digital ledger recorded across many computers
explanation: Transactions are grouped into blocks and copies of the ledger are kept by many participants, making records hard to alter.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Bitcoin is based on which technology?
explanation: Bitcoin records all transactions on a public blockchain maintained by a network of computers rather than a bank.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Bitcoin was introduced in 2008–09 by a person or group using the name:
explanation: The Bitcoin white paper and software were released under the pseudonym Satoshi Nakamoto, whose real identity is unknown.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A cryptocurrency is:
o: Paper money printed with secret ink
A digital currency secured by cryptography and not issued by a central bank
explanation: Cryptocurrencies exist only as digital records on a network and use cryptography to secure transactions.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Each block in a blockchain is linked to the previous one by:
o: Including the cryptographic hash of the previous block
explanation: Because each block contains the previous block’s hash, altering any earlier record would change every later hash and be detected.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The network of everyday objects, such as appliances, meters and sensors, connected to the internet is called the:
explanation: IoT devices collect and exchange data over the internet, for example smart meters and home security cameras.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Contactless toll tags and shop security tags commonly use:
explanation: Radio Frequency Identification tags store data that a reader can pick up by radio waves without contact or line of sight.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A QR code is a:
o: Two-dimensional barcode that can be scanned by a phone camera
explanation: Quick Response codes store information in a square pattern of black and white modules and can hold links, text or payment details.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Technology that overlays digital images or information on a live view of the real world is called:
explanation: Augmented reality adds computer-generated content to the real scene, while virtual reality replaces the real world with a simulated one.

subject: Everyday Science
q: 3D printing is also known as:
explanation: A 3D printer builds an object layer by layer from a digital design, adding material rather than cutting it away.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A drone is technically known as a UAV, which stands for:
explanation: UAVs are aircraft without a pilot on board, flown remotely or autonomously for photography, mapping, delivery and defence.
